passages.title: The Hour Without Bells
passages.passage:
Every Wednesday morning at Hoa Sen Secondary School begins in an unusual way. There is no bell, no assembly, and no teacher standing at the front of the room. Instead, for exactly sixty minutes, the whole school reads. Students may choose any book they like, sit anywhere on the school grounds, and nobody is allowed to ask them a question about what they have read.

The idea came from Ms Thu, the school librarian, who noticed that borrowing had dropped by almost half in three years. "Students told me they had no time," she says. "Between homework, extra classes and their phones, reading had simply fallen off the list." She suggested taking one hour from the timetable and giving it back to books. The head teacher agreed to a trial of one term.

At first, not everyone was pleased. Some parents worried that their children would lose an hour of maths or English. A few students admitted that they spent the first two sessions staring at the same page. But by the middle of the term, something had changed. The library was running out of popular titles, and students had started swapping books with each other in the corridors.

The school has also noticed some effects it did not expect. Teachers report that Wednesday classes are calmer, and several students who rarely spoke in lessons have joined a new book club that meets at lunchtime. "I used to think reading was something you did for a test," says Minh, a grade 9 student. "Now I read on the bus, in the queue, everywhere."

The trial has now been extended to the whole year. Ms Thu is careful not to call it a success yet. "One hour a week won't fix everything," she says. "But it has reminded a lot of people that reading can be a pleasure, and that was the whole point."

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: A lunchtime book club started by grade 9 students
How a school library lost half of its books in three years
A school's weekly reading hour and the effects it has had
Why parents at Hoa Sen are against changes to the timetable
questions.explanation: Every paragraph returns to the sixty-minute reading hour: where it came from, how people reacted, and what changed. The library, the parents and the book club are details, not the main topic.

questions.q: Why did Ms Thu suggest the reading hour?
options: Because students had complained about too much homework
Because the school had bought too many new books
Because the head teacher asked her to find a new activity
Because fewer students were borrowing books from the library
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says she noticed that borrowing had dropped by almost half in three years. The head teacher only agreed to her idea; he did not ask for it.

questions.q: Students must read their books inside the library.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says students may sit anywhere on the school grounds, so the statement contradicts the passage.

questions.q: Ms Thu has worked at the school for more than three years.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The three years refer to the fall in borrowing, not to how long Ms Thu has worked there. The passage never says when she joined the school.

questions.q: The phrase "fallen off the list" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to:
options: become too expensive
been forgotten by teachers
become less important to them
been banned by the school
questions.explanation: Ms Thu is explaining that homework, extra classes and phones left no room for reading; it had dropped out of students' priorities. Nothing was banned or cost money.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the new book club?
options: It meets every Wednesday morning during the reading hour
Its members are required to swap books with each other
It was planned by Ms Thu before the trial began
It attracted students who were usually quiet in class
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says several students who rarely spoke in lessons joined the club, and lists it among effects the school did not expect. It meets at lunchtime, not during the reading hour.

questions.q: In the last sentence, "that" refers to:
options: reminding people that reading can be enjoyable
the number of books in the library
extending the trial to the whole year
fixing every problem at the school
questions.explanation: "That" points back to the clause just before it: the reading hour has reminded a lot of people that reading can be a pleasure, which Ms Thu calls the whole point.

passages.title: Football Where Running Is Against the Rules
passages.passage:
Imagine a football match in which nobody is allowed to run. The ball moves, the players move, but the moment anyone breaks into a jog, the referee blows the whistle and gives the ball to the other team. This is walking football, and it is one of the fastest-growing sports in Britain, though it is played mostly by people over fifty.

The game was invented in 2011 by a football club in the north of England that wanted its older supporters to stay active. Its rules are simple. Teams have five or six players, the pitch is small, the ball must stay below head height, and there is no physical contact. Matches last about twenty minutes each way, which sounds short until you have tried walking quickly for that long.

The sport's popularity has surprised even the people who started it. Today there are more than a thousand clubs across the country, and national tournaments attract hundreds of teams. Doctors have begun to recommend it to patients recovering from heart problems, because it raises the heart rate without the sudden stops and jumps that make ordinary football risky for older bodies.

For many players, however, the health benefits are only part of the story. "I played every weekend until I was forty," says Ray, sixty-eight, who now captains a team in Manchester. "Then my knees gave up and I thought that was the end. Walking football gave me my Saturday mornings back." Players often mention the friendships they have made, and clubs say that members who live alone are the ones who almost never miss a session.

Not everyone approves. Some critics argue that a game without running is not really football, and a few players have been known to bend the rules when the referee is not looking. But as Ray puts it, "At my age, being told off for running too fast is a compliment."

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How a club in the north of England won a national tournament
How Ray recovered from a serious knee injury
Why ordinary football is dangerous for everyone
A slower form of football and why it appeals to older people
questions.explanation: The whole text describes walking football: its rules, its growth, its health and social benefits for older players. Ray is only one example, and the passage never says ordinary football is dangerous for everyone.

questions.q: According to the passage, what happens when a player runs?
options: The player is sent off the pitch
The match is stopped for twenty minutes
The other team is given the ball
The player must leave the club
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1: the referee blows the whistle and gives the ball to the other team. Twenty minutes is the length of each half, not a punishment.

questions.q: Walking football was created to help a club's older fans keep fit.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the game was invented by a club that wanted its older supporters to stay active, which matches the statement.

questions.q: Ray had an operation on his knees.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Ray only says his knees gave up. The passage does not mention any operation, so there is no information to confirm or deny the statement.

questions.q: The phrase "gave up" in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to:
options: became much stronger
surrendered to the other team
were replaced by new ones
stopped working properly
questions.explanation: Ray played every weekend until his knees gave up and he thought it was the end of football for him, so the knees had failed. "Surrender" is the usual meaning of the phrase, but it does not fit here.

questions.q: Why does the writer say that twenty minutes each way "sounds short until you have tried walking quickly for that long"?
options: To criticise the rules of walking football
To explain why some players bend the rules
To suggest that the game is harder than it seems
To show that matches are too long for older players
questions.explanation: The sentence contrasts what the rule sounds like with the reality of doing it, hinting that fast walking for forty minutes is tiring. The writer is not criticising the rules or saying matches are too long.

questions.q: What does the passage suggest about players who live alone?
options: They are usually the weakest players in their team
They value the social side of the club particularly highly
They are the ones most likely to break the rules
They only join because their doctors insist
questions.explanation: Right after mentioning the friendships players have made, the writer notes that members who live alone almost never miss a session, implying the company matters most to them.

passages.title: The Farmers of the Forest Floor
passages.passage:
Walk through a rainforest in Central or South America and you may notice a thin green line moving across the ground. Look closer and you will see thousands of ants, each carrying a piece of leaf many times larger than its own body. These are leaf-cutter ants, and although they spend their days collecting leaves, they never actually eat them.

Instead, the ants are farmers. Back in the nest, the leaves are chewed into a paste and used to grow a special fungus, which is the colony's only food. The fungus cannot survive outside the nest, and the ants cannot survive without the fungus. Scientists believe this partnership began more than fifty million years ago, long before humans planted their first crops.

A single colony can contain several million ants, and each has a job to do. The largest are soldiers, whose powerful jaws defend the nest. Medium-sized workers cut and carry the leaves. The smallest ants ride on top of the leaf pieces as they are carried home. For a long time, nobody understood why. Then researchers discovered that a type of fly attacks the workers while they walk, laying eggs on their heads. The tiny riders act as guards, chasing the flies away.

The ants are also careful gardeners. If a piece of leaf turns out to be harmful to the fungus, the workers stop collecting from that plant within a day or two. They remove diseased parts of the garden and carry waste to a separate area far from the growing fungus, in much the same way that human farmers keep a compost heap away from their fields.

Farmers in the region, of course, do not always see the ants as fellow farmers. A large colony can strip a fruit tree of its leaves overnight. Still, many scientists argue that we have a great deal to learn from an animal that solved the problems of agriculture millions of years before we did.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: How leaf-cutter ants grow their own food and organise their colony
How scientists discovered a fly that attacks ants
Why the fungus cannot live outside an ant nest
Why leaf-cutter ants are a danger to farmers in South America
questions.explanation: The text explains the ants' farming of the fungus, the jobs in the colony and the way they look after their garden. The fly, the fungus and the fruit trees are supporting details.

questions.q: What do leaf-cutter ants eat?
options: Pieces of fresh leaves
A fungus grown inside the nest
The flies that attack the workers
Fruit from trees near the nest
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 says they never actually eat the leaves; paragraph 2 says the fungus is the colony's only food.

questions.q: What is the job of the smallest ants?
options: Cutting the leaves into pieces
Defending the nest with their powerful jaws
Protecting the workers from flies
Carrying waste out of the nest
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3: the smallest ants ride on the leaf pieces and act as guards, chasing the flies away. Cutting is the workers' job and defending the nest is the soldiers'.

questions.q: Scientists understood the role of the smallest ants as soon as they began studying the colony.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 3 says for a long time, nobody understood why the small ants rode on the leaves, so the statement contradicts the passage.

questions.q: There are more soldier ants in a colony than workers.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The passage describes the size and job of each group but never compares their numbers, so the statement is neither confirmed nor denied.

questions.q: The word "strip" in the last paragraph is closest in meaning to:
options: cover completely
remove everything from
climb to the top of
protect from insects
questions.explanation: A colony can strip a fruit tree of its leaves overnight, which explains why farmers are unhappy; the ants take all the leaves away.

questions.q: In the last sentence, "before we did" means before humans:
options: planted leaves in the rainforest
discovered the special fungus
solved the problems of agriculture
began to study leaf-cutter ants
questions.explanation: "Did" replaces the verb phrase just before it: the ants solved the problems of agriculture millions of years before humans solved them.
